title: You're already a leader
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez argues that many people treat leadership as a title to be stepped into rather than a practice that begins in small moments. Prompted by students who avoided her university leadership course because they did not yet consider themselves leaders, she reframed the class around the line 'You're already a leader; let's help you become an even better one.' She lists five everyday behaviours that already count as leadership: noticing problems and taking initiative, building trust and peer influence, self-leadership and accountability, advocating for others, and communicating with care and asking hard questions. The point is that leadership is a journey of refinement without a final destination. The post closes with a coaching pitch, but the argument stands on its own.
points: Treating leadership as a destination granted by title delays people from practising it and fuels the arrogance of those who arrive.
Leadership shows up early in noticing problems and proposing structure, even outside a job description.
Informal influence and honest ownership of mistakes build trust and psychological safety.
Advocating for overloaded colleagues and asking uncomfortable clarifying questions are core leadership acts.
Good leadership is continual refinement with no final destination, so people should start from 'already a leader'.
quotes: Too often, we hand folks a title, but no tools. No support. No clarity on what it means to now be responsible to the people they lead.
A leader can have more direct impact on someone’s mental health than a therapist. Let that sink in.
I was honestly shocked, because the students thought leadership was something you stepped into rather than something you evolved into or became.
It made me realize that, for a lot of folks, leadership feels like a destination rather than a journey.
While it might not be part of our job description, if we’re being proactive, offering solutions or creating structure where it was lacking, we’re already leading.

The key isn’t to not make these mistakes, but to own them. If your colleagues know you’re someone who holds themselves accountable and tries to do better, you’re building a culture rooted in trust and psychological safety—and that’s leadership.

instead of teaching students how they might one day lead, they learned they were already doing the thing. Even better, they learned that good leadership is about continuing to refine our knowledge and approach.
